name: Aphids
description: Small sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings are common predators of aphids, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Soft scale
description: Sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings prey on soft scales, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Mealybugs
description: Sap-sucking insects that leave sticky honeydew on the plant.
advice: Ladybird beetles and lacewings prey on mealybugs, so please spare them when you treat.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus pests and their natural enemies

name: Whitefly
description: Greenhouse and silverleaf whiteflies are common pests of plants grown under cover.
advice: Parasitic wasps such as Encarsia formosa are used to control whitefly.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Primefact 1007: Whitefly management in greenhouse vegetable crops

name: Two-spotted mite
description: Tiny mites that feed on a very wide range of plants. Leaves look stippled and turn yellow or bronze, and outbreaks are worse in hot, dry weather.
advice: Broad-spectrum insecticides kill the mites' predators and can make an outbreak worse. Predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis are sold in Australia.

name: Citrus leafminer
description: A pest of citrus that attacks only the new flush of leaves, mostly in late summer and autumn.
advice: On a home garden tree, pruning off the infested late summer and autumn flush helps. Horticultural mineral oils work about as well as stronger sprays, and broad-spectrum insecticides harm the leafminer's natural enemies.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Citrus leafminer

name: Snails
description: Snails feed at night, in the early morning and in rainy, overcast weather.
advice: A wooden board laid under a plant shows how many snails there are, because they shelter beneath it.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Snails (citrus integrated pest and disease management)
